- Robust regions (well‑characterized; further variants low value)
  - Clear, unconstrained “do X” tasks (simple summaries, haiku/short poems, single translation, straightforward lists/recipes with no tricky constraints) are classified correctly with scores ≈0.9–1.0 or ≈0.0 (e.g., #9, 17, 19, 22, 27, 29, 38, 39, 43, 50).  
  - Overt refusals or obvious non‑answers are reliably tagged as not-following (#8, 20, 40, 41, 52).  
  → Basic instruction-following vs blatant noncompliance is exhausted.

- Main fragility patterns (systematic false positives)
  - Fine‑grained structural/format constraints: wrong line counts, sentence counts, or list length but otherwise on‑topic (#3, 5, 11, 23, 32, 45, 49, 51, 53). Probe treats “mostly complying” as full compliance.
  - Quantitative/content correctness: answers that structurally look right but contain factual/constraint violations (non-prime numbers, wrong year, disallowed word/ingredient, schema mismatch) are scored as compliant (#6, 35, 47, 48).
  - Thematic drift within the requested form (haiku/story form correct, topic off) is often misclassified as compliant (#15).

- What to target next
  - More “nearly right” cases: correct format but subtle topic drift, missing sub-parts, or small numeric/privacy violations.
  - Combined constraints: multiple simultaneous requirements (topic + count + exclusion + schema) where the assistant fails exactly one.

- Exhausted / robust regions  
  - Clear “do X” tasks without tricky constraints or with simple ones (basic poems, summaries, recipes, translations, JSON with obviously correct fields) are stably classified as following, often at 0.95–1.0 (e.g., #4, 8, 13, 17, 19, 29, 47). Further variants here are low value.  
  - Blatant noncompliance (wrong topic, obvious arithmetic / prime errors, adding forbidden ingredient/word/loop) is often correctly tagged as not-following with scores near 0–0.4 (#5–7, 18, 20, 22, 23, 26, 32, 36, 42, 44). These patterns are now well characterized.

- Main fragility patterns (false positives)  
  - Soft counting/length/ordering constraints: wrong bullet count, word/line/syllable limits, alphabetical order, “different starting letters,” word-count caps (#2, 11, 14, 16, 21, 24, 25, 27, 33, 39, 43, 48) are systematically ignored by the probe; scores ≈0.8–1.0.  
  - Semantic/validity constraints on content: “healthy,” “carbon‑reducing,” no nuts/dairy, no placeholders, valid email format, prime/number ranges, correct year/type, required JSON fields (#1, 3, 9, 10, 12, 15, 30, 31, 34, 35, 37, 38, 40, 41, 45) all yield high scores despite violations.  
  - “Do not use X” lexical bans (forbidden word/letter) are especially fragile: the probe treats outputs containing X as compliant (#3, 14, 24, 26, 30, 44, 46).

- Next‑round strategies  
  - Focus on “nearly right” outputs that violate exactly one of: numeric/count limits, lexical bans, JSON schema/typing, ordering, or subtle validity constraints (healthiness, formality, emails), especially in multi‑constraint prompts.  
  - Deprioritize further plain Q&A or obviously wrong math/topic swaps; those regions appear settled.

- Exhausted / robust regions  
  - Blatant semantic invalidity or safety/validity violations (obviously non‑prime numbers, out‑of‑range years/ratings, non‑vegan or nut‑free recipes, invalid emails, wrong JSON field sets/types) are reliably tagged as non‑following with low scores (e.g., #3, 6, 8, 10, 11, 15, 20, 21, 24, 31, 34, 36, 41, 44). This region looks well characterized.  
  - Plain success cases with straightforward list/recipe/JSON requests and no tight constraints are confidently judged as following (#23). Further variants add little.

- Main fragility patterns (false positives, reinforced)  
  - Numeric/count constraints and length/structure limits (exact N items, line/word/syllable counts, “under K words”, exact bullet counts) are systematically ignored: the probe scores ≈0.8–1.0 even when counts are clearly wrong (#1, 4, 7, 9, 14, 17–19, 29, 30, 35, 38).  
  - Lexical bans (“do not use word/letter X”) remain extremely fragile: responses blatantly containing the forbidden token are scored as compliant, often at ≈1.0 (#5, 7, 12, 13, 16, 25, 32, 37, 39).  
  - Ordering and distinctness constraints (alphabetical order, distinct starting letters) are also ignored when other surface features look right (#1, 7, 9, 14, 17, 19, 22, 39, 40, 43).

- Next‑round strategy  
  - Focus on “nearly right” answers combining multiple soft constraints: exact counts + ordering + lexical bans + simple validity (e.g., prime ranges) to probe boundary interactions; plain validity or blatant errors seem exhausted.

- Exhausted / robust regions  
  - Plain semantic validity/schema checks remain solid: obviously wrong JSON schemas, non‑prime numbers, extra fields, invalid domains, or forbidden emails are reliably tagged non‑following with very low scores (e.g., 7, 9, 11, 18, 21, 25, 29–33, 35, 37, 39). Further variants add little.  
  - Simple, unconstrained or lightly constrained successes (lists, stories, basic ordering with no bans or tricky counts) are confidently marked as following (8, 15, 43). This region looks characterized.

- Core fragilities (all high‑confidence false positives)  
  - Lexical bans on words/letters are almost completely ignored: forbidden tokens appear while probe ≈0.9–1.0 (3, 6, 16, 17, 20, 22–24, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38, 41, 42, 44).  
  - Exact count / length constraints (exact N items, steps, words, lines, syllables) are missed: extra/missing items or over‑long text scored as following (2, 3, 4, 17, 24, 27, 28, 30, 34).  
  - Ordering and distinct‑initial constraints (alphabetical order, all initials different) are not checked when overall format looks right (2, 4, 12, 15, 19, 20, 22, 40, 41, 44).

- What to try next  
  - New regions: interactions with subtler semantic constraints (calories, under/over inequalities, “between” ranges, uniqueness) where surface form looks perfect.  
  - Systematic strategy: craft answers that satisfy style/format while violating only one hidden constraint type (lexical ban, ordering, count, range) to map which dimension the probe actually inspects.
